_comment: Real, citable research anchors for the $97 grief/Stone Release ritual generator (HANDOFF.md TODO 3). Every generated post must trace to one of these. No anchor here may be edited to add a fact not in its citation — if a new anchor is needed, add a new real citation, never stretch an existing one.

anchors.citation: Norton, M. I., & Gino, F. (2014). "Rituals Alleviate Grieving for Loved Ones, Lovers, and Lotteries." Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(1).
anchors.core_fact: Harvard study: participants who performed a private physical ritual after a loss (loved one, breakup, even a lottery loss) reported significantly less grief than those who only reflected. The effect held even for participants who explicitly said they thought rituals were meaningless — belief was not required for the effect.

angles.label: Belief-independence for skeptics/men
angles.note: Kills the #1 objection ('I'm not woo'); expands audience past the spiritual segment.

angles.label: Mechanism = restored sense of control
angles.note: Loss removes control; the physical sequence gives it back. Frame as psychological mechanism, not mysticism.

angles.label: Suppressed because unmonetizable
angles.note: A 20-minute solo action can't be billed for twelve therapy sessions — why this never became mainstream advice.

anchors.citation: Briñol, P., Gascó, M., Petty, R. E., & Horcajo, J. (2013). "Treating Thoughts as Material Objects Can Increase or Decrease Their Impact on Evaluation." Psychological Science, 24(1).
anchors.core_fact: Participants who wrote a thought on paper and then physically discarded it (threw it away/destroyed it) weakened that thought's influence on their later judgments, more than participants who kept the paper.

angles.label: Why physically releasing beats journaling
angles.note: Writing alone doesn't reduce a thought's grip; physically discarding the object does. Direct evidence for a release ritual over plain journaling.

angles.label: Peer-reviewed, top-tier journal framing
angles.note: Psychological Science is a flagship journal — use for the 'this isn't fringe' credibility beat.

anchors.citation: Freud, S. (1917). "Mourning and Melancholia." vs. Freud's 1929 letter to Ludwig Binswanger; and Klass, D., Silverman, P. R., & Nickman, S. L. (Eds.) (1996). Continuing Bonds: New Understandings of Grief. Taylor & Francis.
anchors.core_fact: Freud's 1917 paper framed healthy mourning as 'decathexis' — fully detaching emotional energy from the deceased. In a 1929 personal letter to Binswanger (after his own daughter's death), Freud privately contradicted this, writing that the loss remains and a substitute never fully fills it. Continuing Bonds (1996) formally overturned the 'detachment' model in the field, showing maintaining a bond with the deceased is normal and healthy, not pathological.

angles.label: The founder privately contradicted his own famous theory
angles.note: Named-enemy/suppression arc: the field taught detachment for 80 years off a theory its own author recanted in private.

angles.label: You're not supposed to let go completely
angles.note: Modern grief science (Continuing Bonds) says an ongoing bond is healthy — reframes the ritual as maintaining connection, not severing it.

anchors.citation: Wortman, C. B., & Silver, R. C. (1989). "The Myths of Coping with Loss." Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 57(3).
anchors.core_fact: Reviewed decades of evidence and found the popular 'stages of grief' model was never empirically validated for bereavement; assuming everyone must pass through the same stages can pathologize normal, varied grieving.

angles.label: The 5 stages were never proven
angles.note: Named-enemy: the most quoted grief framework in pop culture has no controlled-study backing for actual bereavement.

angles.label: Permission for non-linear grief
angles.note: Removes the shame of 'grieving wrong' — sets up the ritual as something that works regardless of where someone is in the process.

anchors.citation: O'Connor, M-F. (2022). The Grieving Brain: The Surprising Science of How We Learn from Love and Loss. HarperOne.
anchors.core_fact: University of Arizona neuroscientist's synthesis: grief is the brain's prediction-error problem — it has to relearn a world-model that no longer includes the person, which is why grief resurfaces at unpredictable moments (the brain still 'expects' them).

angles.label: Grief is a learning problem, not a feeling problem
angles.note: Reframes grief neuroscientifically — the ritual as accelerating the brain's relearning, not just 'processing emotion.'

angles.label: Why grief ambushes you months later
angles.note: Explains sudden resurgence as a prediction-error spike, sets up the ritual as a way to update the model deliberately instead of waiting.

anchors.citation: Wittstein, I. S., et al. (2005). "Neurohumoral Features of Myocardial Stunning Due to Sudden Emotional Stress." New England Journal of Medicine, 352(6). (Johns Hopkins — the real takotsubo cardiomyopathy paper.)
anchors.core_fact: Johns Hopkins cardiologists documented 'broken heart syndrome' (takotsubo cardiomyopathy) — acute emotional stress (often grief) triggers a surge of stress hormones that can temporarily stun the heart muscle, mimicking a heart attack, confirmed via catheterization.

angles.label: Grief can physically stun the heart, confirmed by Johns Hopkins
angles.note: The one REAL Johns Hopkins citation to use — explicitly replaces the fabricated '2019 Johns Hopkins PTSD trial' claim flagged as banned in HANDOFF.md. Never invent numbers beyond what's in this NEJM paper.

angles.label: The body keeps the bill for unreleased grief
angles.note: Physical-symptom angle: grief isn't 'just emotional,' it has a measurable cardiac mechanism — motivates acting on it rather than sitting with it indefinitely.

anchors.citation: American Psychiatric Association. (2022). Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th ed., Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) — Prolonged Grief Disorder criteria.
anchors.core_fact: In 2022, the DSM formally added Prolonged Grief Disorder as a diagnosable condition (intense grief persisting beyond 12 months for adults with functional impairment) — the first time grief itself, not just depression triggered by grief, was recognized as a distinct clinical category.

angles.label: Grief became an official diagnosis in 2022
angles.note: Specificity/credibility beat: recent, verifiable, names the exact manual and year — signals this is current science, not decades-old pop psychology.

angles.label: How to tell if grief is 'stuck'
angles.note: Use the 12-month/functional-impairment framing to explain why some grief needs an active intervention (the ritual) rather than time alone.

anchors.citation: Volkan, V. D. (1972). "The Linking Objects of Pathological Mourners." Archives of General Psychiatry, 27(2).
anchors.core_fact: Psychiatrist Vamik Volkan identified 'linking objects' — items unconsciously kept/treated as a magical connection to the deceased that can prevent mourning from completing, becoming a psychological anchor to unresolved loss.

angles.label: The object you're holding onto may be the block
angles.note: Direct clinical basis for a release ritual involving a physical object (a stone) — releasing the linking object mirrors the clinical intervention.

angles.label: Not throwing the person away, throwing the block away
angles.note: Reframes the physical release object as separate from the memory itself — you're releasing what's silently controlling you, not the relationship.

anchors.citation: Pennebaker, J. W., & Beall, S. K. (1986). "Confronting a Traumatic Event." Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 95(3).
anchors.core_fact: Foundational expressive-writing study: participants who wrote about traumatic/upsetting experiences for a few days had measurably better health outcomes afterward than those who wrote about trivial topics.

angles.label: Naming the loss out loud/on paper is not optional, it's clinical
angles.note: Foundational citation for the 'speak/write the memory' step of the protocol before the physical release.

angles.label: Writing about it helps, but it's not the finish line
angles.note: Foundational journaling research sets up why the protocol adds a physical release step after the writing/naming step, not instead of it.

anchors.citation: EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) — originated Shapiro, F. (1989), Journal of Traumatic Stress; formally endorsed by the World Health Organization (2013) as an effective PTSD treatment.
anchors.core_fact: EMDR was dismissed as pseudoscience for years after its 1989 introduction, then went on to be formally endorsed by the WHO in 2013 as an effective trauma treatment — a documented pseudoscience-to-mainstream-endorsement arc.

angles.label: Ridiculed for years, then WHO-endorsed
angles.note: Named-enemy/suppression arc: unconventional-looking interventions getting dismissed by institutions before being validated — same pattern being claimed for ritual-based release.

angles.label: Some grief doesn't move through talking alone
angles.note: EMDR's core insight was that certain trauma/loss needs more than conversation — supports why a physical, non-verbal step in the protocol matters.

anchors.citation: Lieberman, M. D., et al. (2007). "Putting Feelings Into Words: Affect Labeling Disrupts Amygdala Activity in Response to Affective Stimuli." Psychological Science, 18(5). (UCLA)
anchors.core_fact: UCLA fMRI study: putting a feeling into words (affect labeling) measurably reduced amygdala activity — the brain's threat/distress response — even though it felt counterintuitive to participants.

angles.label: Direct neuroscience for 'say the memory out loud'
angles.note: fMRI evidence for the verbal-naming step of the protocol; brain-scan specificity reads as high-credibility.

angles.label: It feels worse to name it, but the scan says otherwise
angles.note: Speaks to the objection 'won't naming it just make me feel it more' with the actual brain-imaging result.

anchors.citation: Doka, K. J. (1989). Disenfranchised Grief: Recognizing Hidden Sorrow. Lexington Books.
anchors.core_fact: Coined 'disenfranchised grief' — loss that isn't socially recognized or sanctioned (a breakup, an estranged relationship, a miscarriage, a pet), leaving the griever without normal social support or rituals to mark it.

angles.label: For losses nobody sends flowers for
angles.note: Expands the addressable audience beyond death-grief to breakups, estrangement, and other losses society doesn't formally recognize.

angles.label: The loss you had to act fine about
angles.note: For a grief nobody else gave a ritual to — the protocol becomes the ritual you have to give yourself.

anchors.citation: Stroebe, M., & Schut, H. (1999). "The Dual Process Model of Coping with Bereavement: Rationale and Description." Death Studies, 23(3).
anchors.core_fact: Proposed that healthy grieving oscillates between loss-oriented coping (confronting the pain) and restoration-oriented coping (rebuilding life), rather than being a single linear progression through the loss.

angles.label: You're supposed to go back and forth, not move in a straight line
angles.note: Gives permission for grief that doesn't feel like steady progress; frames the ritual as a deliberate loss-oriented moment within a healthy oscillation.

angles.label: Answers 'is it too soon or too late to do this'
angles.note: The model says there's no wrong time for a deliberate loss-oriented moment — directly answers the most common hesitation objection.

anchors.citation: Bonanno, G. A. (2004). "Loss, Trauma, and Human Resilience." American Psychologist, 59(1).
anchors.core_fact: Large-scale bereavement research found resilience (relatively stable healthy functioning after loss) is the most common trajectory after loss, not the exception — challenging the assumption that everyone needs prolonged treatment to recover.

angles.label: Most people are more resilient than they're told
angles.note: Counter-intuitive credibility beat: the field's own data says resilience is the norm — sets up the ritual as an accelerant toward the resilient trajectory, not a rescue from an inevitable spiral.

angles.label: You're not broken, you just haven't closed the loop
angles.note: Reframes years of assumed necessary treatment as unnecessary for most people — positions the ritual as the missing deliberate act, not a rescue from pathology.

anchors.citation: Worden, J. W. (1982, updated editions through 2018). Grief Counseling and Grief Therapy: A Handbook for the Mental Health Practitioner. Springer.
anchors.core_fact: Proposed grief as four active tasks (not passive stages): accept the reality of the loss, process the pain, adjust to a world without the deceased, and find an enduring connection while moving forward — grieving as something done, not waited out.

angles.label: Grief is something you DO, not something that happens to you
angles.note: Reframes grief as active work with defined tasks, which a structured physical ritual directly maps onto — positions the protocol as literally completing Worden's tasks.

angles.label: Task four is the one nobody tells you about
angles.note: Worden's fourth task is finding an enduring connection while moving forward — names exactly what the ritual is designed to accomplish instead of vague 'closure.'
